stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Says Operation Vivaldi Has Retaken 277 Square Kilometers in Donbas as Starlink Restrictions Hamper Forces
stories.summary:
Ukraine's counter-offensive, code-named Operation Vivaldi, has liberated 277 square kilometers (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region over recent months, according to Ukrainian commanders speaking to the BBC. The operation blunted a Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the Ukrainian-held Fortress Belt cities. Kyiv says it inflicted 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in September, while suffering few losses itself.

The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers acknowledged the Ukrainian advances and voiced fears of further losses. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the gains. Russian Defense Ministry briefings say only that forces are "repelling attacks" near Lyman or "improving the tactical position at the front." The Ukrainian claims on casualties and territory have not been independently verified.

The advance has come even as Russia pummels Ukraine from the air this month, crippling energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians. At the front, Russian drones remain ever-present; one unit commander said his men face about 10 on an average day. Ukrainian forces rely on layered drone systems, including net-dropping interceptors, with live video feeds sent to command bunkers.

Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink network, is integrated throughout these operations. Ukraine said this week, as Vivaldi concluded, that restrictions were imposed on the system without warning, limiting its capability. Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, but it is vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones, and the episode has raised concerns about depending on a tool that can be restricted at short notice.

stories.headline: Update: Albanian Protests Turn Violent in Cities Across the Country
stories.summary:
Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades, the BBC reported. Government buildings and some private businesses have been attacked. A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, along with other government institutions. Dozens of police officers have been hurt.

The unrest began Tuesday as a student movement demanding action on high education fees, book costs and the cost of living, and was joined by secondary school pupils. Clashes have spread beyond Tirana to Durres, Shkoder, Lezhe, Vlora, Gjirokaster and Korce. Masked protesters threw stones, and police responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons. Anger intensified after images of a young man with a broken leg being carried away; officials apologized, but that did not calm the situation.

The violence follows months of anti-government "Flamingo" protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama, now in his fourth term. Those demonstrations began over a Kushner-linked mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast and drew crowds for some 135 consecutive days. Corruption allegations against ministers and senior officials have grown louder, with one deputy prime minister having fled the country and another ordered to step down as investigations continue.

Protesters say they have no party ties, with slogans targeting both Rama and opposition leader Sali Berisha. Several young demonstrators told the BBC that months of peaceful protest were met with ridicule, prompting this more violent phase. Europe is watching closely, as Albania is viewed as one of the leading candidates for EU membership.

stories.headline: Musk Settles Two Lawsuits Over 2024 Million-Dollar Voter Giveaways
stories.summary:
Elon Musk has agreed to settle two lawsuits over the $1 million check handouts his America PAC made to battleground-state voters in the 2024 election, according to court filings published Thursday. The suits were filed in the Western District of Texas. They accused the Tesla and SpaceX chief executive of defrauding voters through the giveaway.

The settlement terms were not detailed in the excerpt available. The program, which offered payments tied to a petition supporting constitutional rights, drew scrutiny at the time from critics who said it amounted to an improper inducement to register or vote. Supporters of Musk argued it was a lawful promotion of political engagement.

The resolution comes weeks before the midterm elections, in which Musk's political spending has remained a prominent subject. The case was covered by The Hill, Bloomberg and PBS NewsHour.

stories.headline: NYC Comptroller Urges Anthropic to Delay IPO Over AI Safety Risks
stories.summary:
New York City Comptroller Mark Levine is calling on Anthropic PBC to delay its possible initial public offering because of artificial intelligence safety concerns. Levine, who oversees city pension investments, said the company needs to address safety work and mitigate risks now, before it faces shareholder pressure to perform. He made the remarks on Bloomberg Surveillance.

The call comes as Anthropic has reported a revenue surge ahead of a planned listing, a development that has already moved Asian technology stocks. It also follows regulatory scrutiny of AI safety, including Federal Trade Commission civil subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic over safety incidents and a lawsuit by eight states against OpenAI over ChatGPT safety claims.

Levine's argument centers on the incentives public markets create: once listed, he said, management would face quarterly pressure that could crowd out safety investment. Anthropic has not been reported to have responded to the comments. Whether the company proceeds with a listing, and on what timeline, remains to be seen.

stories.headline: Collins and Jackson Clash in Testy Final Maine Senate Debate as Control of Chamber Hangs on Close Races
stories.summary:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson held their final debate Thursday night in a race that is one of a handful that will determine Senate control. The exchange grew heated when a protester, shouting about AI data centers, interrupted the candidates. Collins said the heckler was "obviously one of Troy's supporters," and Jackson replied, "Oh, shut up. I don't even know that kid." The debate closed a marathon series of tense encounters between the two.

Collins also used the debate to defend her record. She said she does not regret voting to confirm Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as Health and Human Services secretary. "I agree with him on some issues; I don't with others," she said, crediting him with helping expedite the release of low-income food assistance. She also said she had tried to block the confirmation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The same night, Alaska's Senate candidates clashed in another high-stakes debate. Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is seeking a third term, and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola argued over the Iran war, soaring consumer prices and personal credibility. Both contests will help decide control of a closely divided chamber.

Democrats have argued that Republican incumbents have sided with the president over voters on tariffs and the Iran war, which they blame for higher costs. Republicans have stressed their records and have benefited from large super PAC spending. With Election Day weeks away, both parties are treating the Maine and Alaska races as pivotal.

stories.headline: Democratic Senate Candidates Post Record Fundraising Numbers Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
Democratic Senate candidates posted very large third-quarter fundraising totals, according to FEC data analyzed by Axios. Texas Democratic nominee James Talarico raised $64 million in the quarter. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio, told of the figure, said, "Oh my god, holy crap. I mean, that's a number that's mind-blowing."

Republicans hold an advantage in super PAC money, but Democrats lead in hard dollars from individual donors. Analysts read that gap as a sign of greater enthusiasm among Democratic voters. Talarico faces more than $158 million in outside spending from Republican leadership and Elon Musk as he challenges Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. He has framed the race as a David-versus-Goliath contest against billionaire donors, corporate PACs and the Washington establishment.

Many Democratic ads accuse Republican opponents of siding with the president over voters, particularly on tariffs and the Iran war, which Democrats blame for rising costs. Republicans counter that they hold the advantage in outside spending and point to their candidates' records. Separate reporting this week described a state-backed influence campaign targeting Democrats online and growing use of AI-generated content, more often by Republicans than Democrats.

The fundraising totals come as total midterm ad spending has passed $10 billion, and with the Senate majority in play in several states.

stories.headline: Israeli Settlers Attack Palestinian Olive Harvest in West Bank, Injuring 12 Including US Citizens
stories.summary:
Dozens of masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest near the village of Abu Falah in the occupied West Bank. A local official said 12 Palestinians were injured, including four dual Palestinian-American citizens. A foreign journalist was also hurt. A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks.

Victims described being assaulted with guns, rocks and nail-studded sticks. Majdi Fheed, an American citizen, was treated for deep head wounds, and his elderly mother was also injured. Three cars were burned. A US State Department spokesperson said Washington condemns "criminal violence by any party in the West Bank" and called for investigations, arrests and convictions.

The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more settler attacks than the whole of last year's harvest season. Farmers have taken to stripping trees quickly at sunrise and harvesting in groups from several villages for protection. All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.

The attack follows Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi's call this week for Israel to halt what he called the forced establishment of settlements. Israeli officials have generally said they act against violence by settlers where evidence exists, while settler advocates blame Palestinian hostility and security concerns.

stories.headline: US Measles Cases Top 4,000, Largest Outbreak in 35 Years, With Pennsylvania at Epicenter
stories.summary:
The CDC has confirmed more than 4,000 measles cases this year, the largest outbreak of the virus in 35 years. Nearly a fifth of cases are in children under five, and more than 90 percent are among unvaccinated people. Pennsylvania is the epicenter, with more than 1,100 cases, five measles-related deaths and a possible sixth under investigation.

Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at Penn State Health in Hershey, told PBS NewsHour he is seeing many sick children and babies admitted to his hospital. He described complications including encephalitis, which can leave children confused or unresponsive, and pneumonia requiring oxygen or ventilators. Some infants have been unable to nurse.

Shirey urged vaccination, noting that before the vaccine measles caused three to four million infections a year in the US, with about 50,000 hospitalizations and around 500 deaths. Public health officials say falling vaccination rates in some communities have allowed the virus to spread again.

The outbreak continues to grow, and health officials are expected to keep pressing for vaccination, particularly for young children and in affected Pennsylvania communities.

stories.headline: Fed Chair Warsh Declines to Signal October Rate Move as Investors Pare Hike Bets; Taiwan Weighs AI Chip Export Curbs
stories.summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to say whether the central bank will raise interest rates again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world. Speaking at the IMF meetings, Warsh noted that the Fed has already raised rates once under his chairmanship. His remarks led investors to scale back bets on an October increase, and US equity futures wavered after initially rising.

The Fed's rate-setting committee consists of the seven members of the Board of Governors, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and four of the remaining eleven regional Reserve Bank presidents, who vote in turn. The committee meets eight times a year. The absence of explicit guidance leaves markets focused on incoming inflation data, which has recently shown price pressures building.

Separately, Taiwan is reported to be preparing to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips in order to align more closely with US restrictions on shipments to China. The move comes as the European Union and China hold high-level trade talks. Bloomberg also reported that Russia is deploying networks of bots to spread AI-fabricated videos aimed at influencing views ahead of the US midterm elections.

The Fed's next decision and Taiwan's formal announcement on chip controls are the key developments to watch. Both bear on global borrowing costs and on the technology supply chain at the center of US-China competition.

stories.headline: Trump Invokes Executive Privilege in Kennedy Center Court Fight
stories.summary:
The White House is asserting executive privilege to block some records of President Trump's communications from being shared in an ongoing lawsuit over the future of the Kennedy Center. A White House lawyer argued that information about the president's management of the center, including efforts to add his name to it, should be off-limits to the plaintiffs.

The suit was brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio member of the center's board. She is challenging plans to close the performing arts center for renovations and to add Trump's name to the institution.

The White House lawyer said the privilege would also cover Trump's conversations with advisers who do not serve in government. That position is likely to draw scrutiny, since executive privilege has traditionally protected deliberations among officials. Critics of the administration may argue the claim is being stretched, while the White House frames the records as protected presidential communications.

The court will now have to decide how far the privilege extends in a dispute over a cultural institution, which could shape what documents become available as the case proceeds.

stories.headline: China's Wang Yi Tells Israel's Herzog to Stop 'Forced Establishment' of West Bank Settlements
stories.summary:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Israeli President Isaac Herzog to stop the "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said. The two met face to face on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday. Wang called the Palestinian question "the greatest historical injustice of this century."

Wang said the immediate priority is to fully open access to Gaza and halt a continuing humanitarian catastrophe. Beijing has long backed a two-state solution and is positioning itself as a Middle East mediator, having brokered the 2023 Iran-Saudi deal and joined Pakistan earlier this year in proposing a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran.

Herzog said on X that the talks focused on bilateral relations and regional conditions. He stressed Israel's desire for peace alongside strategic threats, chiefly from Iran and its proxies. China maintains close ties with Iran and is the largest buyer of Iranian oil. Critics note China faces its own accusations of diluting minority populations in Tibet and Xinjiang, which Beijing rejects.

A year into the Gaza ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable. Progress on the deal's next phase is stalled, with Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violations.

stories.headline: Update: Four GOP Senators Join Bipartisan Call for Pentagon Probe of Ukraine Starlink Disruption
stories.summary:
Four Republican senators have joined Democratic colleagues in asking the Pentagon inspector general to investigate reported disruptions to Ukraine's access to satellite data. They are pressing the Trump administration on whether Pentagon officials ordered restrictions on Ukraine's use of the Starshield network.

Ukrainian officials said temporary speed limits on the network limited their ability to intercept Russian drones. Ukraine relies on fast data speeds to operate drones and fixed-wing aircraft on the battlefield, and says the limits disrupted military missions.

The letter comes as Ukraine seeks winter energy and air-defense support while Russian strikes intensify. The bipartisan nature of the request signals unease within the president's own party over the issue, though the administration has not publicly confirmed that any order was given.

The inspector general must now decide whether to open an inquiry. The outcome could affect US-Ukraine relations at a time when Kyiv has accused Washington of withdrawing support.

stories.headline: Houthi Missile Attack on Yemeni Presidential Palace in Aden Kills Five
stories.summary:
Five people were killed and 16 injured when five ballistic missiles struck al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government, officials said. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt. Health Minister Qasim Buhaibeh said the casualties included guards and civilian employees at the site.

The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said the group struck what it called the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden. Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the attack as cowardly and vowed that government forces would continue operations against the Houthis on the south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines. A Saudi-led coalition backs the government and is providing air support for a pro-government offensive.

The attack comes amid sharp escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. Last Saturday a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade. The coalition said it intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region on Thursday, though the Houthis denied attacking Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Rayed Krimly accused Iran of encouraging the escalation by arming and training the Houthis. Iran has denied supplying weapons and says it supports the group only politically, while its foreign minister said Tehran is ready to help facilitate talks between Riyadh and the Houthis. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July when the Houthis announced a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia.

stories.headline: Update: Ship Attacks Near Strait of Hormuz Reach Weekly Record as Oil Exports Slow
stories.summary:
Twelve vessels reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz between 5 and 11 October, the most in any week since the US-Israeli war with Iran began, according to BBC Verify analysis of UK Maritime Trade Operations data. The previous week saw 10 reported attacks, and four more have been reported so far this week. Six ships were struck on Sunday alone.

One of Sunday's attacks hit the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin with a drone near Oman's Sohar Anchorage, more than 250km from the strait. Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two remain missing, according to a seafarers' union. On Tuesday the container ship GFS Pride sank after being hit by an unknown projectile, and its 21 crew were evacuated. Iran's Revolutionary Guard published footage of the sinking and said the ship carried contraband on an unauthorised route.

Experts say Tehran is trying to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military escorts more tankers through the southern part of the strait. US Central Command said commercial traffic continues to flow with coordinated protection from US forces and regional partners.

Oil flows have nonetheless slowed. About 12.6 million barrels per day passed through the strait on 13 October, according to Kpler, down from 15 million at the end of September and well below the pre-war baseline of roughly 17 million. The slowdown adds pressure to energy prices already driving US inflation.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Abandons Energy Truce and Strikes Russian Refinery as Trump Calls Move 'a Disgrace'
stories.summary:
Ukraine attacked a Russian oil refinery after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was abandoning an energy-target ceasefire that President Trump had demanded last Sunday. Kyiv said Moscow never honored the truce and continued its own attacks.

Trump called the renewed Ukrainian strikes on refineries a disgrace and said Zelenskyy is more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin. Coverage describes the relationship between the two leaders as nearing a new low after days of public exchanges. Ukraine also said satellite internet via Starshield, the military version of Starlink, had resumed at previous speeds for the moment after earlier speed limits that Kyiv said hampered its defense against Russian drones.

The collapse of the truce removes a short-lived pause in attacks on energy infrastructure, which has been a central feature of the war. Russian strikes had left about 600,000 people without power in Ukraine despite the announced ceasefire. Supporters of the administration's approach say Trump is pressing both sides toward a settlement, while Kyiv and its European backers say Moscow was never constrained and that Ukraine has the right to hit refineries that fuel Russia's war effort.

stories.headline: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Confirms She Did Not Pass the Bar Exam
stories.summary:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said late Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam, after questions arose about her legal background before joining the Trump administration. Zacharia had previously claimed to be a lawyer, and President Trump has described her as an attorney. The scrutiny came during her first week in the job.

BBC reporting noted she does not appear to be registered with the legal bar in any state where she has lived. A spokesperson for the State Bar of California told NBC News the bar cannot confirm whether it has received a complaint or is conducting an investigation, citing confidentiality rules. A different group had asked the bar to investigate her.

The White House referred reporters to a post by communications director Steven Cheung, who criticized the group that requested the investigation. Administration allies have framed the questions as a partisan attack on a new spokesperson, while critics say a public official misrepresenting credentials raises credibility concerns. Zacharia's tenure began amid the announced resignation request involving Kimberly Guilfoyle, which she disclosed at a briefing.
